utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning. May we have the appearances today, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, my name is Di Fazio, I appear for the Prosecution together with Ms. Korner, and our case manager this morning is Jasmina Bosnjakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Before we bring in the witness, we have a small preliminary matter to raise. It relates to the Prosecution's motion for addition of a number of documents in relation to Christian Nielsen who we believe and who we hope will be able to testify before the recess, the last witness before Christmas, and according to the rules, the expiration of the time limit for the Defence to respond, I think, is on the 14th of December. That, however, would be probably quite late, probably at the moment when Nielsen will be on the stand. So my question to the Defence teams is if they would be good enough to indicate if they have objections to addition of these documents, and if they have objections, could the Bench, on an exceptional basis, ask the Defence counsels to expedite their filings so that we can have the whole thing settled by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we -- we received the batch 96 late last night. I'm actually reviewing the documents right now. It is my belief that we will -- we will provide, if we have any objection, by end of this week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And Mr. Pantelic. Mr. Pantelic, do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Same position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very good of you. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draganovic. Before I invite Mr. Cvijetic to complete his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Good morning to Mr. Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we mentioned an individual who had been killed in Manjaca. His name is Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. His name was Omer Filipovic. Perhaps I in error mentioned his brother's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's all right. Now, you testified about his death in the earlier trial, so I won't dwell on this, but my question is this: Did the competent military organs investigate the circumstances of his death on the premises of Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was killed, when Omer Filipovic was killed, and Bender Esad, around 10.00 that morning, probably at the urging of the camp commander, I observed and saw people in military uniforms coming to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That is sufficient. I will not dwell on Manjaca any longer. Perhaps I interrupted you now, but thank you in any case. And I will not really insist on Manjaca, but I would just have another issue that I would like to raise about Manjaca. You mentioned and you claim that 5.434 camp inmates actually went through Manjaca. You claim that exact figure.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that this was not information and statistics that you had, rather, that it was something that another camp inmate from another camp actually preserved. His name is Ibrahim Begovic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The figure that you came up with on the total number of inmates in Manjaca you also did by actually judging how many pieces of bread, how many slices of bread you had to prepare for any particular day. Does that mean that you actually worked in the mess hall or the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a while I was employed or I worked in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I will not -- I will complete my questioning about Manjaca now. It is not my intention to belittle the number of victims that were there or in any way to show disrespect for their number. I am not claiming that that was a hotel, and I do not wish in any way to try and ease or actually relativise your impression and what you went through in Manjaca, but I cannot agree with your claim that it was a death camp. Namely, even the statistic that you came up with, which is an exact figure, actually speaks to the contrary. If out of 5.434 inmates of that total number, if I try to add up the figures that you mentioned yesterday, the people who were killed and who died in -- in Manjaca, then the figure that I come up is 99.75 per cent of inmates who actually survived Manjaca. Fortunately you were one of them. Would you agree with me that this factually contradicts what you have claimed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you, and if you like, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, thank you. I've listened to your evidence here for seven or so days, and let me put to you my conclusion and perhaps you can agree with me. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over several days you spoke about your tragic position, the very unfortunate conditions there, but let me just say what I observed. Not knowing the number of people who were killed there, I believe, judging your evidence, that at least 50 per cent of the inmates had been killed, but I see that that's not the case. And this is not something that I would like to insist on, and I don't want to actually stir up some memories and the experience that you went through there, but it is my responsibility as a Defence counsel to explore this.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me just mention a little thing that I failed to mention yesterday of the -- when I spoke about the people who were killed there, and maybe I made an error, using some names in error. I mentioned the person Delalic, and I think I said Esad, but it won't be Esad. I think it was actually Husein, his brother, Husein de-Lalovic [as interpreted]. This was a Bosniak a police. There was another person, Emir, his first name; his last name was Mulalic. He was a Bosniak, a policeman, and I just wanted to add these names to the list that I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, what I would like to note here is that optimists will probably work with a figure that I brought here and -- and put forth here, and pessimists will probably use the figure that you've actually pointed to, but we don't have to agree on this.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me just tell you that for the hundred days that I was there, I faced death every single day, and for all these reasons I mentioned that. The situation changed later in the camp, that's for sure. But first hundred days while I was in the camp, every single day I faced death, and not only me, but everyone else, and that is why I said that at this time this was a death camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I said that I didn't want to stir up any memories, but I just wanted to say that, you know, out of optimism, I would mention this. And the Chinese have a saying. They say, "God knows what good that will do." In other words. Had you stayed in Sanski Most and not been in Manjaca, God knows what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that -- and I feel responsible before God and before those people who actually survived and went through all this, it is my duty to speak the truth here. And I also have to say it is not easy for me to give evidence here against the man with whom I spent my childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I believe you are referring to Mr. Zupljanin, but let me tell you now how optimistic he is about his situation at the detention unit. This will -- I will go on a tangent, but just briefly. Of the people who were killed, who died and who committed suicide, both of our clients say that they enjoy -- or, rather, we enjoy all the highest standards in the detention unit, but we complain because we're not free. So it is possible in a situation like this to be optimistic. Would you agree with me? All right. I will move on to another topic. Yesterday, I expected you to answer my question about the civilians, Serbs, who were killed in 1995 in Sanski Most. I expected that you will tell me, while giving evidence, that you're aware of this document and what your position on this document was, but you said that you couldn't recall it, so it is my responsibility now, and I've -- actually, this is what I owe to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, I would like now to give you the page and the transcript number. This --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have document 1D01-0370 up on the screens. Yes, that's it. Can we see it in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the title of this -- this document? Can you remember it? If not, just say so freely, and we're going to move to the next page and then we can remind you of it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we then please turn to page 2, the next page. Mr. Draganovic, on this page 2 you can see that this is a publication. You can see who published it, who published the preface. I assume you know some of these people. For example, Mr. Krstan Simic is now a judge in the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if I'm not mistaken. Can you now see what document this is?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity to see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we then look at the next page, please. Can we look at the following page in English as well, please. Can you please read out these names so that I can see if you will remember this now? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, could I just say something before this proceeds any further. Your Honours, I first saw this document this morning, and I've just cast my eye over it briefly. From my initial look at the document, it seems to be a list of Serbs who -- who -- were killed in the Sanski Most area. Some of the names are undated; many others are dated. Many of them relate to the period 1995, 1998, some from 1996. So they all seem to relate in the main, the deaths, to the period that's right outside of our indictment period and years after the events that we're dealing with here. Now, if there's some other forensic issue other than tu quoque, which is not really a forensic issue, but if there's some other issue that's going to be addressed here using this document, then of course I have got no objection. But if the purpose of this cross-examination is simply to issue to the Trial Chamber and to the witness that a lot of Serbs also were killed, then I've got an objection to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not. Of course not, Your Honour. The Prosecutor must be patient so that I can put my question in relation to this list. This is not a new document. This document is Defence exhibit that was tendered and admitted in the Brdjanin case. It had a different number, DP81B. It was admitted as an exhibit, and this witness commented on the document. So my questions are not directed for the purpose mentioned by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, my first question: Do you remember now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, notwithstanding that it was exhibited -- that it was an exhibit in the earlier trial, the basis of Mr. Di Fazio's objection is that so far such questions as you have asked do not indicate on the face of it the relevance to this trial, and it is that in respect of which I would invite your response before you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I haven't even put my question yet. I asked the witness if he now remembers whether he was ever shown this document, and I'm going to tell you why. The witness conducted investigations into war crimes when he returned to Sanski Most. My questions have to do with investigations into war crimes on which he really spoke about in detail. I cannot reveal to you in advance what I'm going to ask the witness. I do not have the intention to follow the tu quoque line of questioning. I want -- I have no intention at all. I want to ask the witness directly, but first of all I must ask him if he remembers whether this document was shown to him in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Proceed one step at a time, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first step.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you now remember if this document was shown to you by my learned friend Mr. Ackerman, who was a Defence counsel in that case?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember, because it's been a long time since then, since that trial. Perhaps I saw that document as a witness here, but I really cannot remember whether I did or didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, compared to yesterday, I do have a reference.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- excuse me, but if you're asking me about the names of these people --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will ask you. I will ask you. Just one moment. Compared to yesterday, I do have a reference. I'm going to tell you the page. I can see my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio laughing, smiling. Any way, this is page 953 of the transcript of the 23rd of May, 2000 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this is your response to questions by my learned friend Mr. Ackerman. So my question to you now is -- it's the 23rd of May, 2002. That's the date. Sir, did you conduct investigations in these cases, and was anyone charged or processed because of the deaths of these people?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply have no answer to your question now. I don't remember the persons now. I don't even know. I don't remember what I said then, because my recollection was fresher then. I would like you to remind me what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to tell you. On the page that I refer to, amongst other things you said: "I am not sure --" you were speaking about number 2, Pero Grubor. "I am not sure. I think that I did conduct an investigation. I think so, but I'm not 100 per cent sure."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have I reminded you now?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that is correct.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is what I'm stating now. I do remember being at the on-scene investigation when the body of Mr. Pero Grubor was found. I identified the body, and conducted the investigation. I drafted a report and I sent it to the appropriate organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. What I'm interested in is this: Was anyone prosecuted because of Pero Grubor or any other person from this list?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know very well which organs are authorised to prosecute such things. Certain prosecutors' offices and certain prosecutors. I don't know to this day if anybody was charged or not. There is a war crimes department of the prosecutor's office in Sarajevo. There are district and cantonal prosecutors' offices that are authorised to prosecute such things, so I really cannot know that. I don't remember. I have been a lawyer for the past five years. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Very well. I'm asking you this because -- because you said -- you told me yesterday that you received a document by the War Presidency of the municipality of Sanski Most to conduct investigations into war crimes. Can you please interpret the contents of that written document. What does it say? What exactly were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are trying to prove something incorrectly. I'm going to say it again, and I said it yesterday, that I was authorised to gather evidence on war crimes, and that is what I did. And I was authorised to conduct certain investigative actions, and this is something different from conducting an investigation. You would agree with me. Conducting an investigation -- well, you know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you keep evidence on the investigative actions that you conducted in relation to this Pero Grubor? No, no. You personally, did you keep it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no reason to keep it personally. I did carry out certain tasks. The documents are with the court or with the prosecutor's office, reports on the investigation, and probably with the cantonal Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now that we're dealing with documents, can you please tell me, these documents that are accompanying your testimony and which you commented on, I noted carefully the documents that you said you found and where you found them and where this document is being kept now. Before this Trial Chamber I am asking you now where the originals of these documents are that you talked about.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: These documents that you provided the Prosecution. Not the ones that I just showed you now but these documents that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each individual document is in a certain location, and so for each document I would have to tell you, if I remember, where it is, but there is a trail. There is a record of the documents, and all the institutions authorised to prosecute war crimes have such a chain of possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, are all the documents being kept in one place, and can they all be accessed in one place?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the documents we are talking about. I spoke about that yesterday. I replied to a question by Mr. Pantelic, I think, that one part of the documents was handed over to the cantonal prosecutor's office. One was given the AID, one was handed over to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And there was another that the interpreter did not catch.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In response to a question by my learned friend Mr. Ackerman of the 23rd of May, 2002, you said that all the documents were in Sanski Most and that you were keeping them, and you even promised my learned friend Mr. Ackerman that if he were to send a defence investigator -- team investigator, you would allow him to see these documents with the permission of the court. I think this is what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. At that time when I gave the statement in 2002, as you said, the original documents that were seen by this prosecutor's office and by other organs, by other prosecuting organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were in my possession. I was keeping the originals. However, after that when I was supposed to leave the court, I handed the -- or the documentation was handed over to the organs. Each specific document that you are asking me about can be found. The original can be found exactly where it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the -- my question is in the context of judicial economy. Could you assist as to how this line of questions is relevant to what this Chamber would have to decide at the end of the day in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am trying, amongst other things, to check the authenticity of the documents that were admitted as evidence. We intend to send our investigator to Sanski Most to compare these documents with the originals to which the witness is referring. This is the purpose of my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And my last question that has to do with the documents is can we get this written authorisation from the War Presidency that you have? Can our investigators get that from you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to request that from the Sanski Most municipality. I don't have that paper now. I didn't think that I would need to keep it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I must remind you of your answer yesterday. You said that you had it. When I told you that you had an oral and telephone authorisation, you said that you had a written authorisation too.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a written authorisation, and this is why I'm saying that the address to which you must send your request is the Sanski Most municipality, the head of the municipality -- or, rather, the person who was the head of the War Presidency was a witness here. His name is Mr. Mirzet Karabeg. You must ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I had the impression that you had at it home with you, but perhaps I was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I have at home is my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just tell you one more thing -- or ask you one more thing about this written authorisation. Were there any restrictions in the sense that you were to investigate only war crimes committed against Muslims, or were you supposed to conduct investigations about all war crimes that were committed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that I did not conduct investigations. I just executed some investigative actions or tasks, and I'm just repeating that again for I don't know how many times. Thus I carried out investigative actions pursuant to the law and pursuant to what can be referred to as grounded suspicion that a crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Although, I think you did not answer my questions, I was specific, and my question referred to this authorisation from the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will move on to the next topic. Yesterday, in answer to my learned colleague Pantelic's question -- MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, I do apologise for interrupting. Just before we forget now that we're moving on to another topic, what is to be done with the document that was produced to the witness containing the list of names, Serb, Serb names? That document that we -- or, I raised an objection about, should at least be marked for identification. Just so we have a record of what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this -- well, the same thing -- the Prosecutor did the same thing yesterday, and he's repeating. He's doing the same thing today. He is the one who is trying to make a decision as to which documents I am going to tender. I am going by the instructions issued by this Trial Chamber. If I put to a witness a document and the witness does not recognise it, then I will not tender it. Now this has happened already on a number of occasions, and I'm not going to tender documents regarding which the witness says he can't recall them, but they -- yes, they were put to him in the Brdjanin case. So now the Prosecutor is trying to make me run counter to your instructions and tender this document. Well -- but if you'd like me to, I'll do it. So I am seeking to tender it, and let's see what you're reaction is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I suggest that as I recall we did yesterday, and I think this is the basis Mr. Di Fazio's intervention, so that we have a -- where the transcript is looked at, we don't have documents floating out there, as it were. To maintain the link between the document and the testimony as it runs, that we should at least mark it for identification, and that's what we'll do in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit 1D88 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before I put the next question to the witness, I would just like to draw your attention to something that my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan said, who put the question as to the fate of documents that had been tendered in the course of cross-examination in the Brdjanin case. I selected one of those documents. I assigned it a new number, trying to get over the situation, but I think that your decision regarding the admittance of some 100 or so documents is still uncertain, and I'm not clear as to what happened with those documents. Now, had those documents been admitted, we would not be facing this problem now. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That observation I can say I saw coming, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, yesterday my colleague Pantelic showed you a document that was signed by a certain Milos. I will not tell you more about this right now, there will be other documents signed by this same person, but you denied the contents, the truthfulness of the contents of that document. I'll just remind you. There was mention there of the presence of Green Berets, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you please put it on the screen again just to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can ask my learned friend Mr. Pantelic to help me with this if you insist that we give this document back to you, but in fact, this document is not one of my documents. It is Mr. Pantelic's. This is the document where Milos speaks about the presence of Green Berets and their arming, and you said that this was incorrect. Can you recall now?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember it, but could you please put the document again on the screen so that I can read through it one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. If my learned friend can find that number, exhibit number. I was not going to actually show you this document again. I thought you would remember it. 2D21. I do remember you asked for this to be enlarged so you could read it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I do remember that. And could it be enlarged again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you recall it now? Mr. Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'm reading it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, don't tell me you've forgot the contents since yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't forgotten it, but in fact in my view this is no document. This is just some intelligence data that was probably forwarded through special channels of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, please. You commented on this document yesterday. It is not my intention to put this document to you. I want to show another document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my position is unchanged regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 65 ter document 641. Very well. Perhaps we can just zoom out a bit so that we can see the provenance of this document and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at this document and see who the author of it is. So you will agree with me this is the public security station in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please allow me to just read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm waiting for your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This information from the public security station sent to the Banja Luka Security Services Centre relates to the number of weapons that were surrendered or seized up until, as we can see the date on this document, the 2nd of July, 1992. Now, would I like you to look at the number of automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down the document, because the Judges cannot see the statistics, the number. And especially could we see the English versions, please. So now the Judges can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And also the number -- the quantity of explosives, which is 3.140 kilos. Yesterday, you said in answer to Mr. Pantelic's question that Muslims had hunting weapons at best. It was symbolic, really, their arming. What is your reaction to this information coming from official organs? So not from Milos. This document was produced by the public security station.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that was prepared as sort of report by the chief of the public -- of the public security, Vrucinic Mirko. Now, if you're asking me about the content of this document, I can say that this document, too, is incorrect, inaccurate, and it is aimed to be used for propaganda purposes. First of all, let me just tell you this: This document is dated, if I'm not mistaken, the 2nd of July, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you please just scroll it up a bit. I can't see the top part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It says there the 2nd of July.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the greatest number of crimes in Sanski Most were committed up until that date and in the course of the month of July, crimes against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Draganovic, could you please answer --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Let me just say this. There were 4.000 men, Muslim men, arrested, and you can see the information here. You can see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot question this witness if he's just going to keep on talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Counsel, Witness; question, answer. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, would you please answer my question. So your conclusion is that this, too, is a document aimed at propaganda and that it contains inaccurate information; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now let me put to you a bit of information, and I will ask you to confirm it or deny it. You were an investigating judge, and once upon a time I was a prosecutor. In peacetime the police would proclaim amnesty for citizens who possessed weapons, and citizens then who possessed illegal weapons, and they were given opportunity then to report and surrender those weapons. Now, you would agree with me that the number of weapons that were surrendered was never even close to the actual number of weapons that was out there in the field. Would you agree with me, with this conclusion of mine? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you don't agree. Very well. Now, this information that you see here, would the numbers be far larger if the weapons that were seized by the military were included in this list?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact information, data, but I know that the Muslim people did not possess, did not have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, they didn't have weapons, and this is incorrect; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, this is the -- I don't know what document this is, but there are quite a few. There are quite a few that Mr. Pantelic and I showed you, and you always claimed that they were incorrect, so it is my impression that only the things that you are saying are correct, that that's your position.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not true. I will confirm what is correct and accurate. Now, the information in this document is not correct, is not accurate, and I -- I saw it immediately, the minute I set my eyes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, please, all right. You've said that, now let me move on to another topic. Now, you are an attorney, too, so please bear with me. Now, I would like to touch upon a topic that you've already broached during your evidence when you said that in the course of 1991, after the war broke out in -- after war broke out in Croatia, Muslim -- Muslims and Croats, military conscripts, deserted en masse and refused to comply with the call-up papers, especially when they had to go fight in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also said -- you also said that you knew that at that time the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in effect, and it envisaged that this kind of conduct is a criminal offence; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember saying that, but if that is what it says in the transcript, then I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It is in the transcript, but I'm asking you now. Was this correct? Was the Criminal Code still in effect?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did the competent authorities actually take any measures to prosecute these large numbers of conscripts who did not report when they were called up?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not know of any proceedings being instigated by the military organs except in a few individual cases concerning individuals who were transferred from Manjaca camp to the camp near Bijeljina. I forget the name of that camp -- Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And yet you claim that your personal view is that this is not a criminal offence. So if military conscripts are forced to participate in a war and fight against a people, a nation, that this is not -- that this is not really a criminal offence. Have I interpreted your position correctly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am here to testify about facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well -- but this is what you said. So is that your view?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what's in the transcript, the transcript of 2002 in the Talic-Brdjanin case, then that is what I said then, and that would still be my position today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So your position is that the Muslim military conscripts, if they were to go to Croatia, would actually take sides and -- take sides with one and against another ethnic group, and that for this reason they -- this would not be appropriate. Would you tell me, is this the reason why they didn't want to take part?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that was my answer, if that was verbatim what I said in response to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, no. That's my question. Would that mean taking sides?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't even begin to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Why, according to you, did they refuse to participate in that war?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, military conscripts, Muslims and Croats when they were called up to join the 6th Krajina Brigade to fight in Croatia in Titova Korenica?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were at least -- the reasons were at least threefold. There were at least three reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Republic of Croatia had already decided by that time to declare independence, in other words, to become an independent state. That's number one. Two, I think that not even the military commands insisted at the time that Bosniak -- or, rather, Muslim people and Croatian people go and fight. I think they actually followed the principle of voluntary participation, and I recall -- I have already given the first reason. This is the second reason. The third is the senselessness of the citizens of one state going to war to another and to fight the same people, their own people, because Croats in Bosnia and Croats in -- in Croatia are one people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we look at 1D00-4681.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the English, and then I can put the question to you. Can you please look at the title page, Mr. Draganovic. First of all, I'm interested, can you see up in the left-hand corner what it says?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult. The document is difficult to read. If you have a hard copy, could you please show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can provide you with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you now see better? The date is the 8th of July, 1991. You can see that up in the top right-hand corner, "Party of Democratic Action of Sarajevo." And this is a list of candidates for training as special forces in the MUP of the Republic of Croatia. Can we please just look, because all that follows now is a list with first and last names. Can you please look at the year and the final number, at least on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also have page by page on the screen. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we also look at the same thing in the English version. Just go page by page. MR. DI FAZIO: There is no page -- list of pages in English because it's just -- they're just names, and they can be read just as easily in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. There is no text to be translated. Okay. There is some text at the end, so can we now look at the last page, please. Okay. All right. And can we check if there is this last page in English? All right. Okay. This is the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, what it says there is that the last -- "the list ends with number 463. You will get more entries of this list in seven days." And then there is a signature and a stamp. Did you seen that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here is my question: Mr. Draganovic, on that date and at that time, Bosnia-Herzegovina had a ministry of internal -- yes, just listen to me now and to my questions.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As part of the ministry, there was a school for policemen. If you know, it was at Draca. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The school was attended by cadets, young future policemen, as well as so-called course participants who were there in order to become policemen at an accelerated rate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And all that was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that the democratic -- Party of Democratic Action now was sending military conscript, and you can see that by their date of birth, to Croatia to train there in some special forces during the war?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document. I've never heard of anything like it. I've never heard that a list of candidates existed for special training in the Republic of Croatia and that they were sent by the Party of Democratic Action in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, I'm showing it to you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing it for the first time, and I never heard anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you doubt the accuracy of what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do, because had anything like that happened, I would have perhaps known something about it. But I see here --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, a specific question --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the wrong address for the Party of Democratic Action in Sarajevo here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just tell me whether this could also be a document of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say anything about this document, because I don't know anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to tell you then, and you can please tell me whether my assertion is correct. Muslim military conscripts under the patronage of the Party of Democratic Action went to the front in Croatia and returned with uniforms and weapons and entered units of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets when they returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is my assertion logical?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are really asking me something that I don't know and something that I cannot really say anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say I am asserting, so please tell me whether this is possible and logical.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is not correct what you have just asserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Just one moment. Let me finish. It's possible that some citizens from Bosnia and Herzegovina were in some Croatian units in the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, because people went there and they were employed in the police. Mr. Draganovic, my specific question --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just trying to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My specific question and you answered, do you know if any -- if there were organised groups going to Croatia in this manner? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know nothing like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll bring military experts before this Trial Chamber. We will provide other lists, other information, especially lists on the arming of Muslims from Croatia, from Romania, but you say that you don't know anything about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, perhaps I knew something, but you're not asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going ask you. I'm going to move on. I have another ten minutes, so permit me to put my next question to you. Mr. Draganovic -- all right, we're going back to Sanski Most, 1992, which is relevant to us, spring. You said that you were arrested on the 25th of May and that before that you were replaced as president of the court.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Expelled by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what you said. I'm not denying that that is what you said. There were people being replaced in banks and the public accounting service too.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the Trial Chamber, let us just explain what the public accounting service is. I am going to say, and you will confirm if I said it correctly. That was the state financial institution through which all the payments of social, state, and economic subjects was carried out and which at the same time oversaw all the commercial monetary transactions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You, as the president, noticed this change, and you received an order to change, I think, your account numbers and manner of payment. Can you just please tell us exactly what it was that changed here?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What changed were the accounts, and all the payments were directed from the SDK of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the public accounting service of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the public accounting service in Banja Luka or Belgrade. The account numbers were changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So funds no longer were flowing into Sarajevo. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that change, there was no inflow or outflow of cash.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I'm talking about. All financial transactions via Sarajevo were suspended.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. All the payment transactions of that service were suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At that point in time Republika Srpska existed as a fact. It was proclaimed on the 9th of January. On the 28th it received its constitution and its regulations which called for such changes. Do you consider that to be a legal act, a lawful act?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must disappoint you with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're going back now again to differences in opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But just previously tell us. Was this, according to you, a lawful act or not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an unlawful act. This was a violation of the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this resulted in damage to the finances and the budget of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I really have a hard time understanding how this can possibly be relevant. Can you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to finish the questioning of this witness with two documents about this and nothing more. I'm just asking him whether he considers it to be a lawful act or not, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: According to you, Mr. Draganovic, this is not legal.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already given my answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now show document 1D01-0355 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please just zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the copy, on the left-hand side, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have a hard copy of that decision, I would like to ask to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, since time is running out, this is a decision about your suspension as the president of the court. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the court usher please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And can you start answering. How did this whole thing finish? And I'm going to finish with your cross-examination. I'm not going to bother you any more.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I would need to explain the causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No. I'm going to be specific. This is a cross-examination. I'm going to be specific. Is it true that you were suspended? That is the question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that charges were issued against you? And they are attached to this document. May I just look at the number. I'm sorry, I just have to take the document back from you for a minute. So you were suspended because a criminal report was issued against you for a crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can I just see if the charges have a different number so that we can look at that as well and then I will give it to you, I will give it back to you. The criminal report has a different number, so that is 1D01-0360. 1D01-0360. Shall I give you this indictment now for you to look at it? You probably know it, though.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it. There's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up the English copy so that we can look at the description of the crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can just ask what you need to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I cannot until -- all right. What it says here in the indictment is that you also redirected the funds intended for the budget of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that those funds from the court account, instead of the federation budget, you took out and used for purposes specified in the indictment, and by doing that you caused damage to the budget by appropriating funds in the amount of 187.961.2. Is that what it says in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm saying is that what it says in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not say that in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, then you tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're putting the question. You ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll put it again. It says as an official person deliberately violated the provisions law by overstepping the boundaries of his official position and caused damage to the canton budget in the amount of 187.961.2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the terms did not catch up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not the federation but the canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Convertible dinars. All right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My last question to you now, Mr. Draganovic, is: Is this also something that is falsified and that constitutes propaganda? Just specifically yes or no, time is running out, it's going to be break now.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not wish to answer such a question. It's a provocative question, this is how I am taking it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, you don't have to answer. My last question. All right. I'm telling the Court it's my last question. Are you then competent to give your opinion about the lawfulness of rechanneling funds from the Bosnia and Herzegovina budget to the budget of Republika Srpska if you also are charged with a crime from the sphere of -- of finances?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a financial violation that I committed, and I would commit it again were I in the situation that I was in at that time again. This indictment would never have been issued against me, had I before that not conducted some investigative measures for serious corruption against highly-positioned people in Sanski Most and the canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, you don't have to defend yourself. Just wait, just wait. It's finished. Wait, wait, I've run out of time. Wait, enough, enough. You don't have to defend yourself before this Court.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question. I don't want to owe anybody a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just answer the question. You don't have to defend yourself.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not defending myself at all. I would do the same thing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just give you my conclusion. You are not competent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Counsel and Witness, remember the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, we are wrapping up, so just let me put to you my final assessment.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just please ask me. Put questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, just allow me to give my final comment. Well, your final remarks will be something that you will put in your final statement. Now let me just finish with this. All the documents that I point -- that I showed to you and Mr. Pantelic as well, for all of them you said that they were inaccurate and that they just served propaganda purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not correct. All the documents that have been shown by Mr. Pantelic and by you were not qualified in those terms by me. I did refute or dispute their validity and their content, their accuracy, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, here's my final assessment. It is my view that you are not competent to actually assess the validity of those documents and that you are not competent to be a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. This is the only document that I will seek to tender, because it directly relates to the witness. He recognised it, identified it, but it bears two different numbers, so... Well, perhaps I can help you with this, but just let me look for it. Maybe the witness has it. All right. So one of them was 1D01-0355, and the other one -- would you like to assign a number to this document first?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits 1D89 and 1D90, Your Honours. The ERN number of the second document is 1D01-0360.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just say one thing. Mr. Di Fazio will re-examine, but I deplore counsel declining to let a witness answer a question when he has put a serious allegation against that witness and then doesn't give the witness a chance to explain it. And second, I deplore remarks such as the final, not even, question: "In my final assessment, it is my view that you are not competent to assess the validity of those duties, and you are not competent to be a witness." It's an improper observation by counsel. It's not matter for him. It's a matter for Your Honours in any event. But I think that is a most improper way to end a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Re-examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, in order to get through this swiftly, I'd be grateful if you'd try and keep your answers as brief as possible. I want to deal with the last issue that Defence counsel raised with you, namely the issue of the -- the charges from 2003. I'd like you to explain to the Trial Chamber briefly, briefly and succinctly, what they were about. What was it that you were supposed to have done, and explain to the Trial Chamber so that they understand what the indictment laid against you was about.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I conducted some investigations against some highly placed officials, political officials, and also people who were in power in the Sanski Most canton and in the federation. This was the first serious case charging someone with aggravated corruption, and unfortunately I was the one who was to conduct it. I wouldn't want to mention of names of these individuals here, but as for the indictment against me, it was politically motivated. The description in the indictment is the result of the work of a commission of the Una Sana canton government which oversaw or inspected my work in the court, Sanski Most court. When I conducted these investigations - and this lasted over a period of time - it was my responsibility in the course of this work to provide funding for the court so that it could be in operation, and of course some of the fees, the court fees, I ordered to be channeled to the court account in order to cover the costs and the expenses that the court had. This was done by other presidents of the courts both in our cantons and in the federation, because under the law on court fees of the Una Sana canton, it is envisaged or it is specified that these fees are to be used by the court itself, and this revenue is to provide for its material and financial needs. And I even had verbal approval from the minister of justice to proceed in this way. However, I have to mention here that the funds of the Sana Una canton that were specified in the budget and allocated for the purposes of the work of the court that I presided over had not been provided over a long period before that, and there were even occasions where in six months I would not receive any funding for the work of the court, not a single mark. So I resorted to this method in order to provide for the funding for the work of the court. However, as for the charges regarding donations, that -- they are correct. I actually used funds from another account, and in fact, even after the war when the Sanski Most municipality was liberated and life was beginning to get back to normal in that municipality and people were beginning to come back, on several occasions I actually allocated small sums of money to certain sports organisations in the area. Others did the same thing, and I don't really consider this a major violation, because these, too, were organisations of general social benefit. These charges would never have been brought against me had I not at this time or thereabout, within the court system in our canton, criticised sharply certain decisions regarding payments of war salaries to certain officials, and in this manner, in fact, I came in conflict with some of these individuals who were the main actors in this whole operation. So in fact then I was charged in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in order to place me at a disadvantage when new members were to be elected in the judicial organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, we don't want to go into it chapter and verse, and thanks for that explanation, but the essence is that you were moving funds from one place to another for the purposes of the court, nothing to do with you personally; correct? And that applies to the donations that didn't involve your personal enrichment in any way? The sports clubs.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. And -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was the witness ever convicted for -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And finally, and you heard His Honour's question, what was the outcome of this charge laid against you? And again, brevity, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convicted [realtime transcript read in error "conflicted"]. However, I appealed, and my appeal was accepted by the Supreme Court of the federation, and this case was forwarded to another court to retry it. Over six years nobody acted on this, but I had a problem with that because I wanted this to be brought to an end. So I went to Livno and asked the judge there to call a trial for this. I actually admitted that I had committed this financial violation, and I was fined, so I paid about 4.500 German marks in order to pay for that fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. 37, 24, I believe the witness said that he pled guilty to the charges and was fined accordingly. But maybe my learned friend can -- I wasn't actually listening to the English interpretation, so maybe my colleague can clarify this with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And sorry, while we are on the same topic, just a correction to the transcript. It's page 37, line 19. Instead of I was conflicted, witness said I was convicted. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Anyway, you admitted the financial violation, and did that amount in essence to a guilty plea?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As the president of the court, I admitted this, you understand, but that had nothing to do with my position as judge, if would you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation. Another document that you were shown in cross-examination was a document containing lists of -- lists of people, young men who were sent to -- to Croatia, and during the course of that cross-examination, in fact at page 20 -- 27, counsel announced that they were going to do various things, provide lists and other information, et cetera. And then at the end of that said that: "You don't know anything about that," presumably talking about either the document or the issue of sending young men to Croatia. And you said, "Look, perhaps I knew something, but you're not asking me." Is there anything that you want to say to the Trial Chamber about that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to say that some people did go to the Republic of Croatia. They actually applied there for work at the police of the Republic of Croatia. They applied for a job there. These were people who had been in the police force -- or, rather, they were the National Guards. That's what the units were referred to as. And I do not preclude the possibility that there were some people, both Bosniak and Croat, from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were members of those police structures. As for the army of the Republic of Croatia, I really have no information or knowledge as to that, as to the participation of Bosnians and their membership in the army of the Republic of Croatia. I had no information to that effect or that any training was actually conducted, and this is the first time that I actually hear of it. And I believe and think that this is not actually accurate, this list that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When the document was shown to you, and if you need to look at it again just say so, just say so because we can do that, but when the document was shown to you, you had some misgivings about the address. The address on the document is "Party of Democratic Action, Sarajevo, Marsala Tito Street, number 7." What is it about that address that causes misgivings, if any?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if I could see the document one more time, if I could be shown it. I think that it consisted of 13 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's a long list, and it can be shown --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inclusive, the 13th page being the last page. MR. DI FAZIO: It's ID00-4681. It's a Defence document, so ... and unless I'm wrong, it wasn't even marked for identification, so perhaps it -- at this point it should be. I'm not -- I won't be seeking to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I could help with providing this document. That's the only reason I got up. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. I just need the B/C/S. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So perhaps if we can just look at the top left-hand corner. That's the address on the document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my view that this document is really inaccurate, because why would the Party of Democratic Action of Bosnia and Herzegovina compile a list of candidates for training in special MUP forces? There is no foundation in any regulations or any law or in the platform of that party that would provide for that, and I really consider this list to be planted, as it were, by the Defence, that this is falsified, that this is a forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand your evidence correctly, it's the actual content of the document, what it says, rather than anything to do with the format of the document or the address. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, but the address also is incorrect, the address on the first page, the address of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what it should be? Have you got any idea what it should be or not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of the street now, but I'm certain that this was not the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, I apologise. I'm not quite sure what the status of this document is. But at this stage, it should at lease -- well, I'm not seeking to tender it, but it should be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, if it hasn't yet been marked, then we -- so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P424, marked for identification, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is 1D document. I don't know if -- I think it might create a problem in the future, because if -- I mean, if the Prosecution wants to tender this document as an MFI document -- MR. DI FAZIO: No, no, it's -- being marked for identification doesn't mean it's evidence in this case. It's merely marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, but we are going to seek to tender this document in the future. That is why I'm suggesting that this document be given a 1D number. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. I've got no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And MFI'd for identification. MR. DI FAZIO: No problem at all. As long as it's marked by someone, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But my understanding was that your team did not wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, we wish to tender this document, but this witness says that he doesn't recognise the document. He says that it's a forgery. He just said that it's a forgery. So -- so my colleague, Mr. Cvijetic, and I, myself, didn't thought that it was appropriate that we introduce it through this witness. So -- but we will definitely introduce this document. This is a significant document for our defence. And we have other documents that back up this -- this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the avoidance of confusion, we'll just leave it with the MFI number that we have indicated, that has been assigned. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Right. Last Thursday, the 26th of November, you were being cross-examined about the visit of Mr. Zupljanin to Manjaca, and it was put to you that -- this question was put to you. first you were asked about a gentleman named Zarko Tole, a Croatian military man, and you -- and you said you remember him and you remember he was in Manjaca with you. And you were asked: "Do you know that he was a colleague of Mr. Zupljanin's from before the war, and Mr. Zupljanin visited him on that occasion? Do you know that?" And you said: "No, I don't really know that. I don't know anything about the relationship." So you can't comment on that, and it's your evidence that Mr. Zupljanin only went once time to Manjaca. What about other police officer who came to Manjaca, did they come along to visit old friends who were being held in Manjaca? Was that a common thing? Social visit?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately I have to say that no one came to pay social visits to anyone. We, the inmates who were in the camp, we had all lost our friends, the friends that we had till recently before that. So there were no visits, nor would they have been possible. I've already said that a number of members of the military and the police came to the camp, members of the Autonomous Region of Krajina -- or, rather, the then so-called Serbian Republic. Some of these people, of course, I knew because for many years I had gone to school and then university and then through work I knew some of these people. However, there were no social visits to anyone in the camp, to the best of my knowledge, and I would have known and could have known because I worked in the kitchen and I was in the open, as it were, day in, day out, and I could always know when somebody was called out to come out or when somebody was looking for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you for that answer. Thank you. You were also asked on that Thursday about a number of personalities, police personalities. This is at 3928 in the transcript. I just wanted to see what you say about the positions of various policemen. Firstly you said that when you were taken to Manjaca, the -- you were escorted by a gentleman, a warden named Vujanic, Vujanic, and then you said he was actually commander of the police station. Do you know what his first name was?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Drago Vujanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I would just like to make a correction, perhaps, to the interpretation. He was not the police commander. Rather, he was the commander, komandir in B/C/S, of the police prison, a prison warden. And as far as I recall, during that brief period he was a police commander -- or, rather, an assistant police commander, komandir in B/C/S, at the public security station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. And you also mentioned a gentleman named Milan Ivanic -- rather, the question was put to you that if you knew that Milan Ivanic was commander of the police station, you said he was an assistant chief of police, and then again you repeat that had Mr. Drago Vujanic was the chief. So who was the chief at the time that you were arrested and put into prison?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be precise here when referring to the official titles of those individuals. The chief of the police, in other words, the first man at the public security station in Sanski Most was Mirko Vrucinic. So he was the head or the chief of all police sectors. Everyone else was his subordinate. The police commander, komandir in B/C/S, was a Bosniak, Enver Burnic, who was arrested at the same time that I was, and he hasn't been seen since. So when Bosniaks and Croats were expelled from the public security station, and I'm referring here to police officers, I was no longer aware of the positions of those people who had been assigned to certain leading positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Thanks for that explanation. During the course of the cross-examination over the last few days, there's been mention of an organisation known as Green Berets. I want you to explain to the Trial Chamber, again briefly and again succinctly, what exactly and who were the Green Berets in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Green Berets in Sanski Most there's really nothing much that I can say about them because --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You misunderstand me. I'm going to ask you about that. That's another issue, okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... Sanski Most eventually. But what I -- I just want a general explanation. Someone listening to your testimony wouldn't have known what precisely this organisation is, Green Berets. So explain. Who were they? Not in reference to Sanski Most or your person experiences, but just generally, who were they?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
