utterances.text: The Green Berets were, if I may say so, a regular military complement of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was their position in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. During -- during the course of cross-examination you were asked about the Green Berets, and you said at 3968, that in fact there were no Green Berets in -- in Sanski Most. Earlier, however, you had been asked, at 3962, about a Green Berets training ground at a place called Golaja, and you gave an answer saying that that related to Bosniaks who were surrounded in the villages of Vrpolje, Hrustovo, and Pljevci, and that you'd heard about that particular episode while you were at Manjaca. Now, I don't want to go into the details of the episode of what happened at Vrpolje, Pljevci, and Manjaca. What I want to know is when you were talking about those events at Vrpolje, Pljevci, and Manjaca, were any Green Berets involved?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some local people there who decided not to surrender, and they withdrew. They wanted to defend their village which was in the general area of Vrpolje. These people had the status of an organised force, a Territorial Defence and Green Berets, but only in that area of the Sanski Most municipality. But I've already said, however, that in Sanski Most itself, in the town itself and in its suburbs, there was really no organising of any kind, nor were there any Green Berets except for those who were in Vrpolje village where the local people self-organised, as it were. They refused to surrender when they were called to do so by the police and the army and the Serbian authorities. They put up an armed resistance, and thanks to them and their sacrifice they actually took about 46 soldiers as prisoners, soldiers of the 6th Krajina Brigade, and they began negotiations with the command of the 6th Krajina Brigade. These negotiations were conducted on the 2nd or 3rd of June, 1992, and they -- the outcome was a peaceful resolution, and this group was allowed to leave in an organised manner on buses for the free territory of Bihac under UNPROFOR escort, and then the prisoners would be released, because these prisoners were on the buses with them. This was done without any glitches. This exchange was actually carried out with the help of the UNPROFOR, and all these men had some weapons with them. They surrendered these weapons to the UNPROFOR when they crossed over to the territory of the Bihac district.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were assigned, or there were -- they were -- their status was recognised as members of the fighters of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were they commonly known or spoken about as Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb radio and the Serb command referred to them as Green Berets at that time. The status in that sense was regulated by those people only after the war, pursuant to certain legal procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the 1st of -- Tuesday, the 1st of December, well, yesterday, in fact, you were being asked questions -- anyway, in the course of one of your answers, and this is at 3967, you said this: "I'd like to note here that over those 15 to 20 days in Sanski Most some 18.000 people of Bosniak nationality were expelled from Sanski Most. This was up until the second half of August. And of that number over 4.000 men, Muslim and Croat, had already been detained in camps and detention facilities." And you went on to say that numerous Muslim and Croatian villages had been completely cleansed, houses burnt down, some villages completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then later, at 3990, you said that you didn't know the exact numbers of Serbs who were now living in Sanski Most and that -- that you had arrived at that figure of 18.000 by looking at Executive Board reports of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. I want to show you some other figures concerning level -- population levels of ethnicity in Sanski Most. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown 65 ter 283.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we can see from the front -- the front of this document that this is a Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can you see the date? I think it's irrelevant. It's not for the relevant period of indictment. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, we can, and I will. And it's dated May 1993. You can scroll down and you will see that date. You see? May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And I want you to look at item IV in the document. So it will be IV in the B/C/S and IV in the English. And the English, it's on page 2, so I suppose it's -- yes. There we go. So you see there the figures for --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see them, yes. It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Sanski Most area -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read it out. But the figures that we see there, numbers of Muslims and Croats that have moved out together amount to 27.000; and numbers of Serbs who have moved in amount to 5.000. No --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me. That document, of course, it's dated May 1993, so it must relate to information presumably that existed before May of 1993. Now, have you got any reason to quibble with those figures? Have you got any reason to disagree with what the Ministry of the Interior figures tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is calling for speculation. Presumably exist before May of 1993. I mean, this document from 1993. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, I understand that, and I'm not suggest it's a perfect document, but it's -- it's a Ministry of the Interior document purporting to give figures on ethnic movements in various municipalities. And it -- it seems highly probative. The fact that it's May 1993 -- given what we all know of historical events, it can only be talking about the events of 1992 and population movements that occurred in that time. What else could it be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, there seems to me to be a logic about Mr. Di Fazio's explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but you will see -- yes, Your Honour. But you will see during the proceedings that most of the expulsions are in 1993. So this document doesn't say how many people left the Sanski Most municipality area in 1992. We can just speculate about the number during the first five months, and then how many in 1992. The witness is not a demographic expert so that he could confirm or say something like that. In any case, we will have Ms. Ewa Tabeau testify about the movement of the population in that period. This document has to do exclusively with 1993, and we cannot establish on the basis of this document how many people left in 1992 and how many left in the first five months of 1993. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, the witness said 18.000 himself. I can give you the quote from his evidence. He said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, do you have any information to suggest whether this document is cumulative or temporarily limited? MR. DI FAZIO: No. It's -- I've no -- no information suggesting matters one way or the other. The document speaks for itself. It's presumably been prepared with some degree of attention to detail. Where there's data that is not applicable or unavailable relating to Serbs, for instance, it says so. It doesn't claim to be perfect. For example, in Prijedor it says only about 14.000 Serbs moved in. It's not meant to be a document that is presumably by the authors. It wasn't meant to be a document made with demographic precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. MR. DI FAZIO: That's not the point of it. But taken together with the evidence of this witness, that, well, if he says 18.000 moved out and here you've got a police document saying 24.000 moved out, I wondered if there was any disagreement by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The point as I understood it made by Counsel Krgovic was that this only applies to 1993 and that there might be different figures for 1992. So that is why I asked you whether this was cumulative, meaning that it would cover the number of persons who had left Sanski Most up to and including May 1993. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, the point made by Mr. Krgovic is -- can't be founded, at least from what I can see of the document. This is no -- no -- because it's not, as you say, temporarily demarcated. We don't know if this is talking about May of 1993 or going all the way back. Given the numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's move on. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd like to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence objects to the admission of this document. First of all, it is outside of the time period covered by the indictment, and then you cannot see from it to which period it refers. It refers to 1993. I don't know how much this document can help the Trial Chamber. You've heard the witness who gave his assessment, but there are other ways to establish the number of citizens who left the Sanski Most municipality, and it's not possible to do that through this document. I don't know how much this document can assist the Trial Chamber in that manner. MR. DI FAZIO: Can I just ask one or two more questions that might assist you in deciding this issue, of the witness. Just one or two if Your Honours don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How many Muslims were living in Sanski Most before the outbreak of war -- or at least let me ask, before April of 1992 what were the demographics? Have you got any idea?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the ethnic composition of the municipality in my testimony. As far as I can remember, the total number of the population was about 61.000 inhabitants in Sanski Most municipality. There is an exact figure mentioned in the testimony, but it's about 61.000. Of that, the majority population were Bosniaks, Muslims, and they accounted for 29.000 in the municipality of Sanski Most. Approximately it's 29.000. I remember that, because I was also the president of the municipal electoral commission, and this list from 1991 was used, so I remember this. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, given that evidence, 29.000 Muslims, April of 1992. He says 18.000 moved out. This, on the face of it, police document says 24.000, all Muslims and Croats, by at least May of 1993 had moved out. Now, the numbers marry, and the document more or less marries up to reflect the witness's evidence. For that reason it should be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do I not wish to repeat the objection stated by my learned friend Mr. Krgovic. I have a principled problem, a general problem. I think that it is not in accordance with the proceedings before this Tribunal to introduce new evidence during the re-examination. If this is done, the Defence must be given the opportunity to cross the witness on the basis of that document, and I think that as a -- it is absolutely unacceptable to introduce such a -- such a way of presenting documents and of introducing evidence during the re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just a very short submission. This witness confirmed during my cross-examination that he is not demographic expert. So I really don't know why we are wasting such a time on that issue. Mrs. Ewa Tabeau, demographic expert for OTP, will come as a witness. We shall have our expert, and then we shall clarify all this stuff. Mr. Draganovic is a layperson to discuss with him these -- these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll mark the document for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Pending the testimony of the demographer.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit P425 marked for identification, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. And just to keep matters going on this topic, can the witness be shown 65 ter 292, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The -- perhaps we'll just very briefly look at the front page. Again, this is a Ministry of Internal Affairs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic has an intervention. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, same problem. This is period 1991 to 1995. So how this document can help? MR. DI FAZIO: There's, in this case, I can't remember how many adjudicated facts dealing with population movements as a result of the war. As my learned friends from the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is zero. There is no adjudicated facts. MR. DI FAZIO: I beg to differ. But I don't have the adjudicated facts on front of me, but in any event, notwithstanding that, it's a matter of common knowledge that there was large population movements as a result of the war. This is what these documents deal with. How can it be said that they're irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this case -- I turn to Serbian. [Interpretation] In this case, Your Honour, in reference to my client there is no decision on adjudicated facts. So referring to this document and referring to that particular aspect is absolutely unacceptable. MR. DI FAZIO: There are, for Mr. Stanisic, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can we perhaps cut through this. As far as the Bench views this matter, the issue of the movements was raised during cross-examination, so I think it is acceptable that the Prosecution brings up the matter during re-examination in response to the answers given by the witness during cross-examination. So that settles the issue of whether it is acceptable to bring up the matter of the movements of people. Secondly, on the issue of whether this is relevant, as we have said many times before, this is a matter that the Chamber will decide in the end. So let's see what we can make out of it. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the document is Ministry of Internal Affairs. It's an overview, as you can see. It relates to period 1991 to 1995, presumably published or prepared in Banja Luka in February 1995. I'd like to go to item number 11. It's the same in B/C/S, and should also be item number 11 in the English. It's on page 8. I apologise for not knowing the exact B/C/S page, but it's item 11. And obviously relates to Sanski Most. Okay. There you can see some figures. You've got the 1991 figures of ethnic distribution in Sanski Most. Serbs 25.000-odd, Muslims 28.000-odd, Croats 4.000-odd, and so on. Now, you said that you were on the, I think, electoral commission.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Given that experience and your background in Sanski Most and what you know about the population -- populations in Sanski Most, do you have any reason to disagree with those figures that you see there for 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to look at the numbers more carefully. Sanski Most, 1991, 25.000, and then the percentages. All right. How much are Muslims? Twenty-eight thousand. Yes, this information is absolutely accurate. It's accurate. 1991 is as it's stated here. And I think that this data is absolutely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And then we can see the picture according to this police document in 1995. Have you got any reasons to disagree with the figures there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I do agree with this data. I agree, because I know that about 4.000 stayed, and this was information that was also at the disposal of the humanitarian organisations. So these people were receiving humanitarian aid. And then sometime in September or perhaps earlier, about 2.000 again were expelled to Central Bosnia, and then a larger part of the half that remained was engaged on work duty and were engaged on the front in different sectors. So from late 1991, the army of Republika -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when they entered Sanski Most, found 560 inhabitants of Muslim ethnicity. And I cannot remember how many Croats there were, but it was quite a small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have to disregard this answer of the witness because in my cross-examination on my question when I ask him, How many Serbs were in 1995 when this witness came back to Sanski Most, he said, I don't know. So now he knows how many Muslim and Croats were there, and on my question he doesn't know how many Serbs were in 1995 in Sanski Most. This is -- this is unbelievable. Please disregard this answer. This is unbelievable, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Pantelic can put that into his submissions at the appropriate juncture. If Your Honours please, I'd like to tender the document, and if you're not with me, have it marked for identification, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again for the reasons that we gave for the last document, we mark this for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P426, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, your testimony's now at an end. You are released as a witness. We thank you for your attendance to give evidence, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It was a pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission during this time when next witness is entering, for the record I must -- I'm little bit -- it's completely other issue than this. I'm a bit tired with complaining about the working conditions in this courtroom. Your Honour, for the record, I kindly ask the relevant departments of the Tribunal to have a fair approach with regard to the courtroom schedules. I think certain principles should be followed. For example, the priority should be for the joinder case with four, five, or six defendants in terms of scheduling of courtrooms, and then the same principle should be followed for -- for the other cases. Here in this courtroom we don't have enough working space for both Defence teams. For example, today Stanisic Defence is using four working space; and we, only two. We need at certain stage to bring our legal consultant and case manager. So we simply don't have enough computers in this courtroom. Please do your best to inform relevant departments that -- because at the other -- on the other hand, I know, looking at the tentative schedule, there are empty -- empty courtrooms, Courtroom I and Courtroom III at certain days, when we are sitting here and the other two courtrooms are free. So on several occasions, I raised that matter and nothing is happening. And finally, Your Honour, we are facing on a permanent basis another problem, that is the temperature in this courtroom, Your Honour, and I raised that on many occasions and my learned friend Ms. Korner also raised that. The situation is that the part of Prosecution is under a better air conditions than our part. My special watch, Your Honour, with the temperature shows me that here now we have 25.3 degrees celsius, 25.3 degrees. We are all in our robes. Can you imagine if are outside, you know, sitting in the cafe in the robes at 25.3 degrees. It's unbearable, Your Honour. We don't have fresh air. And also this is a very important matter. This is a very risky environment in terms of new flu that is all around. So please do -- do what you can, Your Honours. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. I hope trust you notify the fact that by virtue of the difference in heights, the temperature up here where the Judges are sitting is probably even higher, but we will sustain the hardship of sitting up here. The issue, I think, is clear. CMSS, is, as far as we are informed, perfectly aware of the fact that all Chambers seem to prefer to sit in Courtroom I or III, rather than to sit in this courtroom. So I think that CMSS is actually trying to schedule hearings in this -- in this courtroom only when there is no other option. It comes at the price of sitting in afternoon sessions, because there is a contradicting preference also expressed by all Chambers that they wish -- that they prefer to sit in the morning. And if you have noticed, I think this trial has gone on so far almost exclusively in morning sessions. We have been lucky to escape afternoon sessions. And the price for that is that sometimes we have to sit in Courtroom II. As far as the temperature is concerned, we can regulate it. There is a possibility that the temperature can be turned down, and you will certainly recall from your experience here, that sometimes it can be freezing cold in this courtroom as well. So let's just live by what we have. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just to complete the record, Your Honour, I would like to borrow Mr. Pantelic's watch for the next session and set it over here because it's very cold on this side, and I dread to think about the cold being turned up. We'd be happy to swap maybe halfway through the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, we will take the break now, and at the resumption we would -- we would call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the -- before the witness comes in, I was just reminded that I forgot to introduce Miss Deirdre Montgomery, our legal assistant. At the start of the actual last session she entered the court, and I missed that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess I should indicate that I came in during the last session and Mrs. Korner went out. I'm Tom Hannis, Your Honour. And while we are waiting, Mr. Pantelic did kindly loan me his watch and I would indicate that since he gave it to me ten minutes ago, the temperature now has dropped to 23.2. Our next witness is ST-110, Your Honours, Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From this submission it seems to me that Trial Chamber is in the best position in terms of temperature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Good afternoon, sir. Could you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 26th of December, 1943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a lawyer, and I work currently as an attorney-at-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we note that from the rule under which you are giving evidence that you have, in fact, testified before this Tribunal previously, and moreover, being a lawyer, you would be familiar with the process of the court, so the -- we would begin, of course, with the side calling you, in this case the Prosecution. Then we will move to cross-examination, and there may be re-examination, and after this, the Chamber itself may have some questions. So with that, I would ask Mr. -- I would invite Mr. Hannis to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You indicated that you had previously testified at this Tribunal, and I believe that was in the Krajisnik case. Prior to coming to court, did you have an opportunity to review your prior testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And having done so, were you satisfied that it was an accurate record of your evidence, and if you were asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers, and as far as I could hear the audio recording, I have no objections and no -- nothing to say about any inaccuracies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would move to tender his transcripts. There are six days of testimony. The 4th through the 8th of April, 2005, as well as the 15th of April, and the associated documents in the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P427.1 through P427.27, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, we know that you were a lawyer. Could you give us a little brief background about what you were doing in 1991 and early 1992. In addition to working as a lawyer, I understand you worked as a judge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 I was an attorney-at-law. I was a judge up until 1990. So in 1991 I began to work as an attorney-at-law, and also in early 1992 I did the same. I was in the same profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see that you were also engaged in politics and were a member of the Assembly in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Assembly of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was elected as a deputy of the SDS, although I was not a member of the SDS. I had to put my signature on signing that I agreed to be on their election list, and I -- and thus I became deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. In addition to what has just been tendered, I understand that one of the exhibits pertaining to this witness 92 ter package has already been marked for identification, and it is P165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, in 1992 did you become a member of the government of the Bosnian -- of the Bosnian Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the government at the end of May 1992. In early April the fighting began in Sarajevo town, and a number of people, a -- who were in the leadership actually moved from the town to Pale. I also had to leave Sarajevo, so I happened to be in Pale as well. And Mr. Branko Djeric, who was the prime minister then, offered a position for me. He offered that I stay in Pale and that I be co-opted into this government. Soon thereafter Mr. Karadzic, as president of the Presidency, decided that my -- on my appointment as the vice-president of the government, or maybe this was verified in early June by the Assembly, I'm not really sure any more how it went, but this is approximately the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just for a matter of guidance and my learned friends, I intend primarily to show this witness a number of government session minutes, and I'm going to go in chronological order. The list I submitted, I think, had originally some 75 documents on it, but because most of those are discussed in his prior testimony, I'm only going to show him about 25 of that original list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, the first one I want to show you is what has already been marked as Exhibit P224. And that will appear on the screen in front you in a moment. It's the 20th session of the government, a meeting held on 3 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could, I'd like to go directly to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you have it on your screen, I'm going to ask you about item number 1. We're talking about the government being informed about current issues. And the second paragraph says: "The government has especially been informed about the lifting of the blockade from the Marsal Tito barracks. They have expressed dissatisfaction with the fact that the Serbian party is not participating in the negotiations because of the fact that has been especially emphasised, Serbian people is most directly interested in lifting the blockade ..." And the last paragraph: "It's been especially emphasised that none has the right to negotiate the issues of importance for the Serbian people without the legal and legitimate representatives of the Serbian people. Serbian people will not allow anyone to behave like that regardless of who that might be." Do you know who that's referring to in this discussion? Who was negotiating about the blockade of the barracks on behalf of the Serbian people who the government apparently did not think should be doing that? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I cannot really read what's on the screen right now. I have a problem. I can only see portions of the text. As for the lifting of the blockade of the barracks, as far as I can recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can hand you a hard copy that might be easier for you to read.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who negotiated the lifting of the blockade of the barracks. As far as I can recall, this was done by some officers from Belgrade. Now, which particular officers I don't really know, but I think they were still the Yugoslav army or whatever the official name of the army was. They were the ones who negotiated this. And I don't know that anyone participated in the negotiations from our part, but if that's actually how it was, I don't know, because this was an issue that was not within my, as it were, purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say officers from Belgrade, are you referring to members of the JNA or ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I remember seeing on television this column leaving the barracks and planes overflying, and I know that up on Pale we were commenting on this and how a large quantity of weapons remained for the Muslims to use in the town, but that's -- that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's page 3 of the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Above item number 3, four paragraphs up, there's a paragraph that reads: "Report about the work of the National Security Service should be prepared and submitted to the government for adopting. Responsible: The Ministry of Interior." Do you know why the government was requesting a report about the work of the National Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't. Surely the government did need to know what was going on in every sense including national security, but how close or how secretive this service, the State Security Service was and how secretive had it had to be, I really don't know about that to this day, whether that kind of report had to be forwarded to government, or presented to the government, and what format I don't really know, but I can see from this text here that it was supposed to be done and submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us how long did you work in your position as the deputy prime minister. From -- from May when you started it until when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Djeric resigned around the 20-something November in Zvornik at an Assembly session, and this meant that the government was dissolved, and -- but we remained in our posts up until January when the next government was put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So from -- from the time of this meeting on the 3rd of June until you left the government, did you ever receive a report from the Ministry of the Interior about the work of the National Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I ever saw such a report myself. I do not rule out the possibility that it was contained in a batch of materials, but I don't think that I saw anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next item says: "A procedure for determining war crimes should be initiated. Responsible: The Ministry of The Interior and the committee for war crimes formed by the government." My first question is who, if you know, was on the committee for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the government appointed a commission for establishing war crimes against the Serbian people sometime in the spring of 1993. I was, I think, it seems the president of that commission. However, that is the next government, not the one that we are discussing. And it's a different story, actually. That commission did not manage to meet and set itself up. Then in May or June 1992 -- actually, I don't know if there was any commission like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your answer you mentioned a commission for establishing war crimes against the Serbian people that was set up sometime in the spring of 1993. Was this commission for war crimes only against the Serbian people or against non-Serbs as well, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was for crimes against the Serbian people. But I said it was never constituted, because in my deepest conviction the intention was not for it to work. Mr. Karadzic told me personally that I would be the president of that commission, and a couple of times I talked with Mr. Krajisnik about how are we going to organise this commission. Where are we going to have it sit? How are we going to work? How are we going to explain to the regional police forces that the commission is to be supplied with relevant material? But this was really never rounded off. It never started to function. Then co-operation on the assembling of documents on war crimes was established with the institute in Belgrade. I've forgotten the name of the institute or the name of the person who headed it, but he co-operated with organs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely Republika Srpska, and with members from the Ministry of Justice and people from the MUP in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn now to another meeting. This one occurred on the 13th of June, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry I may need help from the Registry officer. I think this was part of the 92 ter package it was 65 ter number 1190, and I don't know what exhibit number that has now. Or perhaps it wasn't part of the 92 ter package, and I want to just show it now. 1190.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Trbojevic, are you more comfortable working with a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would like one. It's a little bit too far for glasses, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll ask the usher to help me, and I'll trade you for the one you were just using. You'll see in a second that this is a meeting, as I said, on the 13th of June. It's headed as the 27th session, and it has a list of the persons attending. I note that apparently Professor Djeric was absent, and as deputy minister you presided over the meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the point I wanted to ask you about here is on the very last page, page 5 of the English. Just above the signatures of the secretary and yourself. Two paragraphs -- or two bullet points up. It says: "The government indicated the need for establishing the bodies and taking over of the authority in newly captured areas, which is one of the predispositions for keeping those areas within the republic." Is that a reference to geographical territories that had been taken over militarily by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is formulated like that here as if it was about forming the organs in newly captured territories. I really couldn't tell you which specific areas that referred to. There were no particular instructions as to how to form the organs of authority in these newly captured areas because all the areas were with mixed population. There was no area where the Serbian units or Serbian organs of power were entering for the first time. These were municipalities where already a series of organs were existing and functioning already. So the government pointed out to this need and then people discussed about it, but I don't know what was the immediate reason for this being talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Beyond identifying the need for establishing the bodies and taking over authority in those areas, what was done to see that happen? Did the government establish any committees or propose any action? Do you know what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nothing. I don't know that the government sent a body or a person that would organise the situation in the field. Nothing like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The next bullet point, the last in this minute says: "The government has postponed the consideration of the request by the Ministry of the Interior to barter the steel from 'Metalka' for food ..." Do you know what that was about? How was the Ministry of the Interior involved in trading steel for food?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the specifics of the situation, but generally I know that steel was discussed and that it should be dispatched somewhere, most probably to Serbia, and that some food would be given in return, and I think that there is a dispatch on that where it was said that the Ministry of the Interior cannot be involved in trade, and I think here that they're talking about essential reserves, strategic reserves, and it probably had to be done in that form. I don't know who's firm Metalka is. I don't know what quantities were involved. I know that there was conversation on this topic and how inappropriate it was for the Ministry of the Interior to be appearing in any actions where delivery of goods was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. It goes on to say: "... it was concluded that the matter should be examined and put under the jurisdiction of the taking over the commodity reserves." Do you know what ministry in the government was responsible for the commodity reserves?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was the ministry of trade and procurement. I think that was its full official title. I don't know who was the director of the directorate for commodity reserves. I don't remember. I remember the person, the face, but I don't remember the name. Probably it does appear in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to tender 1190 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand this is part of the 92 ter -- this already has a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I thought it might, but I wasn't sure. Can we have for the record which number it is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P427.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next one I want to show you is P231, and, Mr. Trbojevic, this -- I will again give you a hard copy because that seems to be easier for you. This is a meeting on the 16th of June, 1992, designated the 29th session of the government. The only item I wanted to ask you about in this one is item number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's on page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that has to do with the government giving its support to the draft concept of the wartime information system in the Serb republic of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we'll have to go to either page 2 or 3 of the B/C/S as well. What we've got on the screen now is the agenda which includes item number 6, but I need to see the full commentary about item number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the English, fourth paragraph down it indicates a working group's been established to define and analyse the concept of an information centre with you, Mr. Trbojevic, being designated the group leader to work with Bogdan Subotic, the minister of Defence; and Momcilo Mandic, the minister of justice. Can you tell us, then, did this working group manage to get together and do anything about creating an information centre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that this group never actually met, sat down as a group and reviewed any material or generated any material, nothing ever materialised out of that. All of us here, the only person who actually had some contact in terms of information tasks was Velibor Ostojic. I think he was the minister of information. That was his official post, and he had some people who worked, listened to the radio, the television, followed the press, and wrote what he required. I don't know about Bogdan Subotic and the military, how much they worked with those information centres. I heard that they were such information centres, but I don't know. I think that Momcilo Mandic and I did not really join in any of that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for you, Mr. Trbojevic, it's page 5 of the B/C/S. And if you could go up three bullet points from the bottom. My English says: "The Order on Treatment of War Prisoners. It was decided that it would be released in the media." Do you know who issued that order on the treatment of war prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that I remembered, but it had to have been written by the defence minister, because if it refers to prisoners, then he was the only person who could have written anything on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know why it was decided to release it into the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know to tell you the truth, but there was some logic to present ourselves in nice and good colours, so probably the order was written pursuant to the conventions from the laws on war, and that was probably the sense in publishing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document referred to there has 65 ter number 148, which I believe may have a P number now. And I just bring that to your attention. I'm not going to show that to the witness. He talked about it in his Krajisnik testimony, but I just wanted to make a reference to it now since we were looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Registry confirms that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could she indicate the number for my record?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. It's Exhibit P427.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise for not having caught up with the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next meeting I would like to show you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next meeting I'd like to show you, Mr. Trbojevic, is Exhibit P232. And again I can hand you a hard copy with the help of the usher. We see -- we see you're present at this session, and I want to ask you about item number 10, which I believe is at page 5 in the B/C/S. And the first paragraph there at the very top of your page is translated as: "It's been concluded that the Ministry of the Interior prepare a report on the work of the National Security Service and the Public Security Service and propose measures for a more efficient functioning." In the first one we looked at we saw that there was a direction to the Ministry of interior to prepare a report on the work of the National Security Service, and you told us you never saw such a report if it did come in. But how about this: This also calls for one about both national and public security. Do you know if that report was ever prepared by the ministry of the interior and delivered to the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I received a report or reports by the Ministry of the Interior. I don't know in what period. I don't know whether that -- that contained this part that concerns state security, but I did see some reports, yes. That is definitely so. I even saw a report in which the Ministry of the Interior, with a copy being sent to the Presidency or -- there is a copy sent to the government, and the original goes to the Presidency. I don't know. But I did see some reports, and I can confirm that there were some reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see a report from the Ministry of the Interior dated around the 17th of July in which Mr. Stanisic had reported that the army and the Crisis Staffs were directing that non-Serb civilians be -- be taken into custody, apparently for the purposes of future exchange? Did you ever see such a report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I really could state with a high degree of certainty that I did not, because had I read it, I would have remembered that as something that I would not have expected. So I think such an assertion that there was an order to arrest members of other ethnic groups and to use them for exchanges, I would tend to say that I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you to the last page of this document in both English and B/C/S. There's -- there's a list of people under a couple of regions, and your name is listed as number 1 under the "Serb Autonomous district of Eastern Herzegovina," and it appears from the earlier text that these were work groups that were supposed to go out to the assigned regions and try and help establish more efficient working at that level. Do you recall being named as a member of the work group for Eastern Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no work group for Eastern Herzegovina. I was appointed as commissioner in Eastern Herzegovina, and I went to the Trebinje municipality, Nevesinje and Gacko, on those duties. And then again I went to Herzegovina with the director of the commodity reserves whose name I cannot remember, because they needed to make a decision on the sale of some aluminum that was pulled out of Mostar, and so on. But if that has to do with this previous question about the exchanges of citizens, we didn't do anything on that particular matter, and there was no commission in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall on what date approximately you were in Trebinje in connection with that trip?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was probably summer, June or July. We went by helicopter. It was nice weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last paragraph in this document says: "The government has concluded that all measures being taken promptly for a more efficient work of the Republic Commission for the exchange of prisoners. With regard to this fact, it is necessary to secure the accommodation and other conditions according to a previous decision of the government. (The ministry of justice is in charge)." Do you recall what that previous decision of the government was relating to the work of the republic commission for exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that in the material that was shown to me while preparing for my testimony, I saw that Rajko Colovic submitted his resignation to the post of the president of the commission for exchanges. After that, the president of that commission was a Captain Dragan. I keep forgetting his last name. I think his last name was Bulajic. And as far as I know, all those exchanges were actually under the auspices of the military organs. I don't know that the government adopted any decisions as to these should be exchanged, these should not be exchanged, these should be exchanged more dearly, and these more cheaply. I don't remember any single conversation on that topic, and I don't think that I saw any decision in that sense. But I do know that the commissions functioned as part of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the Ministry of Justice was also involved with the commission for exchange; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they did anything specific. The ministry of justice does have a service that monitors the prisons, so I don't know whether because of that it did have a certain amount of contact with this particular area, but if we're talking about prisoners of war, I don't know that Mandic or Avlijas were inspectors for monitoring the implementation of sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about the Ministry of the Interior? Do you know if they had any role or involvement in connection with the commission for exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you about that is generally what I think about that, but when we're talking about prisoners -- prisons, existing prisons that had to do with the district courts, there were guards there guarding persons who had been taken into custody, and the guards are from the ranks of the police force, and any entrance has to be carried out with the assistance of the police. When we're talking about prisoner-of-war camps, I don't know if the civilian police did or did not and to what extent co-operated in activities of the military police, and the guards from the ranks of the military is something that I can only speculate about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You became aware at some time in 1992, didn't you, that in addition to regular prisoners of war, that is captured fighting men, that there were non-Serb civilians who were being detained and exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically how I could answer that question. It was found out that permission was granted for international journalists and groups to enter Manjaca, and they were permitted to enter Prijedor, Omarska. We even saw footage with a bunch of people who don't look like fighters. This is, I think, my initial information, and I think that's -- that's what it was. So that could be when I found out that there were civilians, because I saw women also in Prijedor, children, so on. That could be the extent of my official knowledge on that matter. Actually, what I knew about it. I don't know that I had any official sources or channels to get information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what about unofficial? Did you have any unofficial knowledge or unofficial sources?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: See, at the time I was Pale, this was summer 1992. We were still in Pale without telephone connections, practically without communication with any particular area. I don't have any business contacts with anyone anywhere. You couldn't get to Banja Luka until the corridor was broken through sometime in July, I think. I came to Banja Luka in late November 1992, and that's when I began to mix and mingle with the citizens, and that was when I was able to hear some things. Before that, really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to now move to Exhibit P233, and I'll trade you hard copies again with the help of the usher. This next one, Mr. Trbojevic, is a meeting on the 27th of June, 1992. It's the 31st session of the government. And the first thing, could you, when you have it, look at the first page where it lists persons attending. I have a question about one of the names. In the second paragraph listing attendees, there's a Slobodan Belasevic in the place of Momcilo Mandic. Is that the name you mentioned earlier as someone who you thought was working with the commission for exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think his name was Slobodan Verlasevic, and I believe this was a colleague who was a misdemeanours judge before the war in Sarajevo, and it is possible that this is a reference to him, but I can't recall really. I don't remember meeting him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if he was working in the Ministry of Justice in late June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't. I don't recall seeing him, although it says here that we attended the same session. He sort of disappeared from view, as it were, and I haven't seen him sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 5 in both the English and the B/C/S. At the very bottom of the page for you, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And near the bottom for us in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says: "Due to the information that there is a variety of centres for military training, the government has concluded that these centres have to be legalised and put under a uniformed command or have to be dissolved." Do you know what the problem was with this, that -- that it came to the government's attention and there was a conclusion that the centres had to be legalised? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. I have no idea what centres for military training this refers to, nor did anyone point this out as a problem, nor do I remember that the government decided to legalise them or to dissolve them. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You never heard mention of a Captain Dragan or Red Berets in connection with this matter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have heard of Captain Dragan, but he was not mentioned as someone who was involved with anything in Republika Srpska. As far as I know, he conducted training in Croatia, but that's as far as I know about it, and I really learned of this, and then I read about it in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If you could go to the next page in your B/C/S, at the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we're still on page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "It has been agreed that this matter be discussed at talks with the army Main Staff." Do you recall the results of any discussion with the army Main Staff about these training centres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said I can't recall any discussions on any type of centres, and this could only -- this is only something that perhaps the minister of defence could tell you based on the information he had at his disposal. As for me, I didn't know of any centres then or later, especially not of any centres that had anything -- that didn't have anything to do with our Main Staff. So there's really nothing I can add to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Continuing on from there: "The government has entrusted the Ministry of the Interior with taking --" and we have to go to page 6 in the English, you're still on the same page, Mr. Trbojevic. " -- with taking away the illegally obtained assets, cancelling all temporary vehicle registrations, except the ones registered for the work of state organs, institutions, and organisations." Do you recall what that was about? What assets had been illegally obtained and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were rumours about legally obtained assets aplenty, and here they specifically mentioned vehicles that were registered, that the registrations had to be verified. There were various companies or enterprises, both public and private who were involved in this, and the government was here trying to actually put some order into all this so that the office for war reserves could know what they had at their disposal. As for war booty and what was obtained in that way, that was really something that could not quite be worked out under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next -- the very next point: "Mico Stanisic, minister of interior, is to go to Bijeljina at once and solve the questions raised regarding the work of the Centre for Security in the autonomous region of Semberija." Do you recall what the questions raised were regarding the work of that security centre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that the Ministry of the Interior was in Bijeljina. Why in Bijeljina, I don't really know. But before the republic ministry took up headquarters in Bijeljina, I don't know what their problems could have been. I'm referring to the portion of the police that was referred to as SAO Semberija, which is what this conclusion would be about. I don't know what the issue was or how it was resolved, but I do know that in the final instance the Ministry of the Interior was headquartered in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see a report from a Ministry of Interior, I think he held the position of inspector at the time, named Dragan Andan regarding work he'd done between late May and, I think the 12th or 17th of June, that pointed out problems in that area? Did you ever see that report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't have it in my hands, nor do I know what it contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Mr. Stanisic actually did go to Bijeljina shortly after this meeting where it was said that he is to go at once?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you at any subsequent government session ever hear him report back to the government about what might have happened in connection with those problems in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that I heard about it. I'm not saying that he did not report to the government, but -- to the Assembly, but I really don't recall it. I don't know what it would have been about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to go to exhibit 427.12, and I'll hand you another hard copy, Mr. Trbojevic. That will be with you in a moment. It's dated the 29th of June in Pale, and the 33rd session of the government. And the only item I want to ask you about concerning this meeting is item number 11. It should be page 5 of the English and the last page of the B/C/S for you. It's current issues, and it indicates: "Rajko Colovic, president of the central commission for the exchange of war prisoners has been dismissed from his post as president." And I think you mentioned that earlier. Do you know why he was dismissed? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I did see a piece of paper where it said that he was submitting his resignation or asking to be relieved, and here I can see that the president of the central commission here was appointed -- Slobodan Avlijas was appointed as the president, and Mladen Mandic, but I don't know that they've actually accomplished anything or done anything in that respect, nor have I heard any shred of information that they had anything to do with exchanges.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure that that is the word that the witness used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether this was one of the proposals that had never actually been followed through, which is probably -- most probably the case, I don't know, but I think that neither Avlijas nor Mandic actually did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple things. The interpretation indicated the interpreter wasn't sure they got the correct word, and I don't know if that referred to your answer about saying you -- "Nor have I heard any shred of information that he," I think that refers to Avlijas, "had anything to do with exchanges." Is what you said, "shred of information"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There's only a slight difference. I didn't hear any information that he did anything or had anything to do with exchanges, either Mandic or Avlijas. I'm not actually claiming this with absolute certainty. It is possible that they did do something in that respect, but I really did not hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wasn't certain from your answer whether you were saying the the commission itself didn't do any work about exchanges after this 29th of June, or whether you were merely saying that, as far as you know, those two gentlemen, Avlijas --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Those two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Mladen Mandic, how is he related to Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they're brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move next to a meeting on the 4th of July. This is exhibit P236. And again I can give you a hard copy. Thank you. When you have that in hand in a moment, you'll see it's -- the minutes are for a meeting on the 4th of July, 1992. It's the 36th session. You are listed as being present. I want to ask you a term about terminology, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's page 2 for you, sir. It's at item number 6. Well, actually, I guess it's the agenda. And number 6 says: "Some questions regarding the introduction of the war regime." It's my understanding that at this time, July 1992, in the Bosnian Serb Republic or the Republika Srpska, at this time there was -- there had been declared an imminent state -- or a state of imminent threat of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Imminent threat of war, yes, that was proclaimed by a decision that was signed by Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1992 in that territory was there ever declared a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In this early period, I think not. There was some pressure exerted by the army and the General Staff -- the Main Staff. They were claiming that it was necessary to declare the state of war, so that the conscripts had to be held to a higher standard, disciplinary standard, when call-up papers were sent to them. Also regarding the possibility of using military companies if needed, and so on and so forth. But the government opposed that, resisted that, feeling and viewing the situation with a more optimistic eye, trying to resolve the war situation as quickly as possible, and also in an attempt to regulate the various relationships between different government agencies. And there was a fear that -- and we feared -- we didn't want the military authorities to get involved in this and to regulate all the areas of life and government. And there was no inclination to introduce a state of war because we felt that this would lead to total anarchy, and that was the position of a few members of the government, including myself. We felt that this was not necessary, and that is why we opposed it. The state of war was introduced for the first time in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps, but I can't tell you exactly when. Later on, it was also declared, I think on the entire territory or -- I'm not really sure anymore, but looking at some of these cases, I know that Karadzic, President Karadzic, did this. He declared a state of war without having the proper authorisation for it, empowerment, but I don't know any -- of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did that happen, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. These decisions were published. I don't know now when exactly this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who under the constitution and the laws in effect at that time had the authority to declare a state of war in -- in the Republika Srpska? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, off the top of my head, I couldn't really say. I did look at this once, and I think you have it written down somewhere during one of the questioning. Whether the Assembly it was or -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Still on page 2, bottom of page 2 in the English, there's number 2 under item 1. It says: "It has been concluded that all ministries propose a general concept on the war regime, as well as the regime of each ministry by Monday (6th July)." Can you explain to me what that term "war regime" means in this context? Is that the manner of working, or what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's something comparable to extraordinary circumstances. So there were rules as to how things were to be done under extraordinary circumstances. There would have to be round-the-clock duty service. You couldn't leave the building without getting approval of that, when you could see clients and when not, and so on and so forth. So that is what is referred to here. The regimen, as it were, was in relation to the fact that there were all kinds of threats from all sides all around us, and in that situation this was an attempt to actually establish the rules of conduct. Some ministries wrote those out, those rules, some didn't. I don't know how it all transpired, but this effort to declare the state of war was a constant effort. There was a set of laws that was proposed to one -- to the Assembly on one of the sessions. This was a situation where imminent threat of war was actually made tantamount to the state of war, and a couple of us actually resisted this. I left. I walked out of this session because I felt that this was inappropriate, that this was actually undermining the state behind the front lines and -- but these laws were passed, and they actually caused a lot of damage. And then later on for years this was discussed one after another, all these items.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if -- I'll ask you a question. If you can perhaps help me understand the difference it made. Whether it was a state of imminent threat of war or a state of war or a state of really bad things were happening, how did that -- how did that change how life worked by the title? I mean, what was the difference between an imminent -- state of imminent threat of war and a state of war? What difference did that make in how the government worked, or how the Presidency worked, how the Assembly worked? Can you explain that for us about that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the term the "imminent threat of war" and the "state of war," those terms are really military or diplomatic terms. They had more to do with the military or diplomacy than with interior policies. Of course there had to be a system of regulations that would kick in, as it were, and become applicable in place of the normal regulations that would apply under peacetime conditions. So they would kick in when the state of war is declared. And as for the interior, the competence of the interior organs, the police, the administration organs, assemblies and so on, they could all be actually put to work under different -- a different set of rules so that their work could be regulated in a different manner, and so on and so forth, whereas the discussion on the use of property and the seizure of vehicles or various machines that belonged to different companies, up all the way to the funds that the banks had, the monies that the banks had at their disposal. All of this could be then put to use for the war effort, whereas this could not be done in peacetime, because in wartime you knew exactly who the authorised signatory was in order to use certain assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in a state of war who would that be, the authorised signatory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be the organ that is given that authority, whatever was proclaimed as that organ. For instance, the unit that would be in that area would have the authority. So it didn't have to negotiate their position with anyone. They could appoint someone by force, as it were, to be, say, a manager of a certain company. So this would be something that the commanders would be authorised to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One last item in this document. It's on page 4 of the B/C/S, and it begins at the bottom of page 4 in the English. Item number 8, Mr. Trbojevic, says: "The question has been raised whether there are agreed criteria regarding the moving out of the Muslim's population from the territory of the Serb republic of BH. "It has been concluded that the government has not until now had a point of view on this matter. The Ministry of the Interior is entrusted with preparing," on to page of the English, "information on this issue that the government would consider and take the appropriate standpoint." Do you recall the discussion about this, criteria regarding the moving out of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no such discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the Ministry of Interior prepare information on that issue for the government to consider and take a standpoint?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that I've seen such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know it's a minute or two early, but this is an appropriate place for me to break, and I would like, on the record, to indicate I'm returning Mr. Pantelic's watch to him. The temperature now on this side is now 20.9 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, we are at the point where we must take the adjournment for today. We will resume in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning. And there is a caution which I'm obliged to give you, although from your past experience you know it quite well, namely that that having been sworn as a witness, you cannot communicate with the lawyers from either side, nor can you discuss your testimony with anyone outside of the courtroom. So we resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm aware of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
